query: Which material can be used for enhanced catalytic activity and durability toward HER and HOR, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) catalyst incorporating non‐noble transition metals such as Mo and W will exhibit enhanced catalytic activity and durability for HER and HOR by tuning its d‐band electronic structure for optimal hydrogen adsorption/desorption and by providing a multi-element matrix that resists electrochemical degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional noble metal catalysts (e.g., Pt-based catalysts) that offer high initial catalytic activity but suffer from limited durability under harsh cyclic electrochemical conditions.
generation.intervention: Design and synthesize a multi-element high-entropy alloy catalyst by incorporating transition metals such as Mo, W, and other compatible elements to fine-tune the electronic structure.
generation.conditions: Typical electrochemical environments for fuel cells or electrolyzers, including both acidic and alkaline media under cyclic operational stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: The alloy’s microstructure and modified d-band electronic structure achieved through high-entropy composition tuning.
generation.mechanism: By altering the d-band center, the modified electronic structure optimizes hydrogen adsorption/desorption kinetics, while the multi-element, high-entropy matrix improves resistance to corrosion and degradation during repeated cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA catalyst will demonstrate lower overpotentials and higher turnover frequencies for both HER and HOR along with slower performance degradation over time compared to conventional Pt-based catalysts.
generation.baseline: Electrocatalytic metrics of standard noble metal catalysts like Pt/C in similar electrochemical tests.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected under controlled experimental conditions; however, the precise degree of performance enhancement and long-term durability will depend on the exact alloy composition and processing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact magnitude of overpotential reduction and durability enhancement, which will depend on optimizing the alloy's composition and microstructure.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA catalyst does not exhibit at least a 20% reduction in overpotential at 10 mA/cm2 and a similarly significant improvement in durability (i.e., ≥20% higher current retention after cycling) compared to the Pt/C benchmark, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. decision.trend: Over the past few years, research on high-entropy and refractory alloys has advanced through systematic control of alloy compositions and processing routes to impart enhanced durability under harsh conditions such as high-temperature oxidation, radiation, and severe mechanical stress. Starting from simpler alloy systems with limited stability, researchers moved to sophisticated processing techniques (e.g., high-pressure/high-temperature treatment, magnetron sputtering) that produce refined microstructures and coherent interfaces. Although these studies have been directed toward mechanical strength, oxidation resistance, and stability under extreme environments rather than electrocatalysis, they established that carefully tuning composition is a powerful lever to overcome trade-offs between performance metrics.
decision.unsolved: Despite the success of these approaches in boosting durability and stability in demanding conditions, the challenge remains in developing a catalyst that is both highly active for hydrogen evolution and oxidation reactions and sufficiently stable under harsh electrochemical conditions. The current state‐of‐the‐art noble metal catalysts still face cost and durability issues, and adapting alloy design strategies to simultaneously optimize catalytic activity and long‐term chemical stability in electrocatalytic environments has not yet been achieved.
decision.lever: Develop a high-entropy alloy catalyst by incorporating non‐noble transition metals (e.g., Mo, W, and similar elements) in a multi-element mix to tailor the d‐band electronic structure, enabling optimal hydrogen adsorption/desorption while providing robust resistance to electrochemical degradation.
decision.why: Given the proven benefits of composition tuning in enhancing durability and microstructural stability under extreme conditions, applying a similar strategy to electrocatalysis is a logical next step. By leveraging the high-entropy alloy concept, researchers can design a catalyst that not only mimics the favorable hydrogen binding characteristics of noble metals but also overcomes their degradation issues under cyclic electrochemical operation.
